name: Number Series — Find the Next Number
whatIsIt: A number series is a list that follows a hidden RULE — your job is to spot the rule and predict the next term. The commonest rules are: add a constant (2, 5, 8, 11…), multiply by a constant (3, 6, 12, 24…), squares or cubes (1, 4, 9, 16…), and 'differences of differences'. The trick is to look at the GAPS between terms first.
whyNeeded: Number series is the single most common reasoning topic in SSC, Bank, Railway and campus aptitude tests. It trains pattern recognition — the same skill behind coding, science and problem-solving everywhere.
realLifeUses: Spotting trends in data (sales rising by a fixed amount)
Predicting the next step in a repeating process

vocabulary.meaning: The fixed amount added each step (in an add-pattern).
The fixed number you multiply by each step (in a times-pattern).
Look at the gaps between terms; sometimes the gaps themselves follow a rule.

story.title: The Gap Between the Steps
story.text: Isha sees 2, 5, 8, 11, __ and freezes. Her coach says: 'Don't stare at the numbers — look at the GAPS. 2 to 5 is +3, 5 to 8 is +3, 8 to 11 is +3. The rule is add 3, so next is 11 + 3 = 14.' Then a trickier one: 3, 6, 12, 24, __. 'The gaps grow, so try times: each doubles. Next is 24 × 2 = 48.' Isha learns to always check the gaps first, then try multiply, then squares.
story.answerInStory: 14 — the rule is 'add 3' (each gap is +3), so 11 + 3 = 14.

visual.caption: Look at the jumps first: 2→5→8→11 each jump is +3, so the next number is 11 + 3 = 14.

teachingGallery.title: Check the gaps, then multiply, then squares
teachingGallery.note: Add-pattern: constant gaps. Times-pattern: gaps grow fast. Square/cube: compare with 1,4,9,16 / 1,8,27.

standardMethod.summary: Find the differences; if constant it's an add-rule; if growing fast try a times-rule; else test squares/cubes or alternating patterns.
steps: Write the gaps between consecutive terms.
If the gaps are equal, the rule is 'add that gap'.
If the terms grow fast, test 'multiply by a constant'.
Else compare with squares (1,4,9,16), cubes (1,8,27), or check alternating/odd-even patterns.

alternateMethods.name: Second differences
alternateMethods.whenToUse: When the gaps themselves change by a constant.
steps: Take the differences of the terms, then the differences of those.
If that second layer is constant, extend it back up.

trickPractice.trick: Gaps first, then times, then squares
trickPractice.intro: Always look at the differences before guessing.

commonMistakes.mistake: Guessing a rule from the numbers alone without checking the differences.
commonMistakes.fix: Always write the GAPS first. Equal gaps → add-rule; fast growth → times-rule. The gaps reveal the pattern almost every time.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forcing an add-rule when the terms are clearly multiplying (calling 3,6,12,24 an add-6 pattern).
commonMistakes.fix: If the gaps keep GROWING, it isn't a constant add — test division: if each term ÷ the one before is the same, it's a times-rule.

challenge.q: The gaps in a series keep DOUBLING. The rule is probably…

questions.q: The first thing to check in a number series is…

teachBackPrompt: Teach a friend the number-series method: write the gaps first. Use 2, 5, 8, 11 (add 3 → 14) and 3, 6, 12, 24 (times 2 → 48), and explain how the gaps tell you whether to add or multiply.

revisionCard.summary: Number series = find the hidden rule. Step 1: write the GAPS. Equal gaps → add that number. Fast growth → check a common ratio (multiply). Else test squares (1,4,9,16), cubes (1,8,27), or second differences (1,3,6,10). Predict the next term from the rule.

gameMission.title: Crack the Sequence
gameMission.brief: Spot the hidden rule and fill the blank before time runs out! Check the gaps, try multiply, test squares — and never force an add when it's really a times.

realLifeProject: Make three number-series puzzles for a friend: one add-rule, one times-rule, one squares. Swap and solve — the puzzle-maker must be able to state the rule.

rememberIt.hook: Gaps first: equal → add, growing → multiply
rememberIt.unpack: Differences reveal the rule. Then test squares, cubes, or second differences.

studentQuestions.q: Where do I start on a hard series?
studentQuestions.a: Always write the gaps between terms first — equal gaps mean 'add', fast-growing gaps mean 'multiply'.

studentQuestions.q: What if the gaps aren't equal or a nice ratio?
studentQuestions.a: Take the gaps of the gaps (second differences), or compare with squares/cubes and odd/even alternating patterns.
